utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. The Chamber didn't have the time to discuss about the Tintor interview's admissibility, so the Chamber will give its ruling on Tuesday next week. Yes, Ms. Sutherland, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, we finished off yesterday when it was put to you that the Bosnian Serb side denied access to repair lines, and you said transcript page 31054: "I personally do not know about that. It was a matter for UNPROFOR. They were the ones who were in charge of this operation and then they would inform us that they had received approval. That was the duty of UNPROFOR and that was what we had agreed upon at Sarajevo airport." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify this, and we're talking about the -- the time period of the conflict. If we look at 65 ter number 24262. Mr. Lubura, this document in front of you is a monthly report July 1993 of the utility situation and repair missions situation details. And if we can go to paragraph 11, please. Now, UNPROFOR says here that -- that the Serbs denied any access to the repair location on the line supplying the town Reljevo-Vogosca. This denial of access is not something you would have heard about, is it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about that. I told you that it was an UNPROFOR obligation to gain approval from both the Serb and Muslim side in terms of any repairs to the distribution lines leading to Sarajevo. It was their obligation. If we established that there was a cut somewhere, the UNPROFOR had to obtain permission from both sides and then two teams, one per side, went in the field to fix it. It was something for them to do. My part was to use my expert knowledge to carry out the necessary repairs. That's the extent of it. I had no connections to either of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you -- on that note, you didn't know first-hand how the damage had occurred. You were just there to fix the damage. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: If there was a cut on the transmission lines in the Reljevo transformer station, we had a surge protection barrier where we could detect where the cut occurred, whether it was a single phase or double phase cut. We could tell, because the instruments showed it to us, the protection instruments.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know that access for repairs being -- were being granted in exchange for concessions from international forces or the BiH side?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, if there was a malfunction and it usually occurred along disengagement lines at Sarajevo airport, both Serbs and Muslims came to agree with UNPROFOR on the date of repairs. UNPROFOR was there to secure a lull --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, that wasn't my question -- sorry. My question was did you know that access was being granted in exchange for concessions from international forces or BiH side? For example, if we look at a document. If we can have Exhibit P00896.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's coming up. It will be one moment. If we can go to page 6 of the document. That's 1 of -- sorry. Page -- yes, page 6 of the document. It says here under "Utilities": "The Serb military continues to insist that there will be no restoration of utilities until the fighting around the city has stopped." Did you ever hear about this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I see this document. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could have a look at 65 ter number 24264, please. This is dated the 27th of September, 1994, from Akashi to Annan, and if we can go to paragraph (b) under Electricity: "Electricity repairs have begun on the Sarajevo network following Karadzic's agreement to clear the access of repair teams provided UNPROFOR subsequently also addressed the problem of the eastern and Northern Bosnia power lines, of particular interest to the Serb civilian populations." Again, this is something that you have heard of or not?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know well that the transmission lines between Reljevo and Kiseljak which had an antenna connection to the Jablanica-Kakanj distribution line, there was a malfunction at Mount Kokoska in the direction of Kiseljak. On that occasion, UNPROFOR obtained approval from all three sides, because on this occasion the Croatian side was included as well as the Muslim and Serbian, and my team fixed the transmission line at Kokoska so that there should be an unhindered supply of electricity to the transformer station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This text suggests that repairs didn't begin until the agreement was given by the accused clearing access. Was this something that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that there was a malfunction at Mount Kokoska on the transmission line there, and we fixed it. UNPROFOR came and we sent two teams in the field. There was another team on the Croatian side from Kiseljak, and we fixed the transmission line at Mount Kokoska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. You can't exclude the possibility that there were political decisions not to -- that -- that there were political decisions to delay or deny the repairing of lines that were feeding into central Sarajevo having seen these documents.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not interested in politics. I'm an electrical engineer. My only job was to maintain and fix electricity facilities that were within my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement at paragraph 15 and yesterday at transcript page 31046 that you didn't have enough spare parts, particularly transformer oil, insulators, switches, distribution devices and protection devices. Were there any cases where parts, for example, transformer oil, were brought in by UNPROFOR but their use was being blocked by the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that UNPROFOR transported much of the spare parts needed for the transformer stations via Kiseljak and Ilidza to Sarajevo. We intervened with UNPROFOR once, and then in 1994 they also supplied us with one-third of the spare parts, whereas the other two-thirds went to the Muslim side. The one-third we received remained in our warehouse --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's not responsive --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- to my question. My question was were there any cases where parts were being brought in but their use was being blocked by the Bosnian Serb side? Do you know of any -- are you aware of any cases?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you were never ordered to cut off electric power to any part of Sarajevo. This is in paragraph 17 of your statement. This doesn't exclude the possibility that other Bosnian Serb authorities cut off electric power.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is speculative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the director of the facility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, what is your point -- what was your point, and what was your basis?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is called to speculate, to guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to respond? I don't think -- let me read your question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a yes or a no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Simply the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the facility manager, I was never ordered by anyone, be it civilian or military authorities, to cut off electricity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As I said, my question was: Does it exclude the possibility that other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic's objection had some basis, because -- if you look at the answers the witness has already given, it may be a truism that it doesn't exclude the possibility, but the answer to that, yes or no, is simply an answer that there may or may not be a possibility. It doesn't advance the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I take your point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, you said you -- you were never ordered to cut off electric power, and -- and you said that you never would. It is true, is it not, that power was cut off by the Bosnian Serbs to the areas in central Sarajevo? Mr. Lubura?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is unclear. What do you mean cut off by the Bosnian Serbs to the areas in central Sarajevo? It is not clear to me. How could the Serbs obstruct supply to the centre of Sarajevo? It's not clear to me. If you look at my grid schematics, you could see that we forwarded voltage from Reljevo to Buca Potok via the distribution line Sarajevo 10 Reljevo and Sarajevo 8 Buca Potok. Had the transmission line been dammed in that part, there would have not been any electricity in the central part of Sarajevo under Muslim control. In other words, that part of the transformer -- transmission line had to be fixed first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there was also -- you were also feeding into -- from Vogosca down to Velesici and Kosevo. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From Vogosca the transmission line Vogosca-Velesici was never fixed. There were attempts to have it fixed but it never was, not until May 1995 when I joined the Energoinvest company. The only transmission line that was functioning, taking electricity supply to the centre of Sarajevo was Reljevo-Buca Potok.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay, if we can have 65 ter number 24253, page 3, please. This is -- this is an UNPROFOR document from -- a UN document from the civil affairs officer to the acting DSRSG in -- dated the 26th of May, 1995, and it says, "This morning --" just at the bottom of what's on the screen now: "This morning civil affairs has been informed by SCS that the electricity supply to the city is cut. It appears that Pale authorities made a political decision to cut electricity supply along the Vogosca and Reljevo lines. If such situation persists Sarajevo will have no water soon." So, sir, this is a contemporaneous document at the time of the NATO air-strikes which shows that a decision was made by Pale to cut electricity into the city.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what date is this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's dated the 26th of May, 1995. If we can go back to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that time I was in Lukavica, and I do not recall this. The manager by that time was Mr. Jovicic, whereas I returned to the Energoinvest company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When -- when did you go to Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of May. I was already in the Energoinvest at Lukavica that day; 1995, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think you said just a moment ago that by May they had fixed the line from Vogosca to Velesici, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't fix that as long as I was the facility manager. That's what I said. The only functioning transmission line was Reljevo-Buca Potok.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we can see here that this document makes reference to -- to the supply being cut along the Reljevo line into the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my testimony, I did say that it was the only transmission line that was operational which could carry electricity from Reljevo to Buca Potok. That means Sarajevo 10 Reljevo and Sarajevo 8 Buca Potok. That transmission line functioned for the most part. 7 Buca Potok, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can have a look at 65 ter number 24254, please. On -- this is dated the 31st of July, 1995, another UN document, a Weekly Situation Report. If we can go to page 7 under paragraph (F) "Utilities." It says: "Serb authorities in western Sarajevo are now willing to talk to their Bosnian counterparts, said they cut the water -- cut off the water, electricity and gas supplies in late May" 1995 "to punish the Muslims for their offensive around the city." You said that you weren't aware of this electricity being cut off in May 1995, but were you aware that the Bosnian Serbs cut off the water on occasions in order to punish the Muslims either for their offensives around the city?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this document is from June 1995. I said that by that time I was already in Lukavica in Energoinvest. Hence I couldn't have known what was -- about what was going on in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, I said that you had previously testified that you weren't there in May. My question was: Are you aware that the Bosnian Serbs cut off the water -- the electricity or the utilities, in fact, to punish the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the document or a reference that this was indeed carried out? This is an interpretation of the talks or negotiations, but was this implemented at all? Ms. Sutherland is putting her questions as if this was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland was asking whether witness knew or not. The witness can answer easily.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to Defence 65 ter exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, how much longer would you need, Ms. Sutherland? Your time was up a while ago, and you seem to not to pay attention to your time at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought that I had 20 minutes -- sorry, 20 minutes this morning. And I note I have an additional five minutes, and I do note that the accused took 45 minutes in chief yesterday as well as tendering a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 1D03405, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is dated the 28th of May, an UNPROFOR Weekly Situation Report. On paragraph -- e-court page 3 at paragraph 6, summarising the events following the air-strikes, it says: "They have cut the water and electricity supplies to Sarajevo." And then if we can go to page 17 -- or paragraph 17 on page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm wondering what is the point of putting documents to him during a time that he wasn't there. This is now the third document. They haven't tendered the first two, neither of them seem to be admissible. What is the point of putting a third one to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, Mr. Karadzic made the interjection that he wanted to know whether in fact it had been cut off and I shouldn't have risen to his bait. This document clearly shows that it was cut off. I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, up until you were in Lukavica, how long were you in Lukavica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. -- yes. Just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The Chamber sees a point in Mr. Robinson's observation. It's difficult to see the point of putting similar documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As I said, I rose to Mr. Karadzic's bait on him wanting to know whether it had been cut off. I was simply showing this document to show that it was reported that it was cut off as was the case with 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I don't see the point of putting the similar -- put documents. Why don't you put your question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I said I would move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, how long were you in Lukavica for? You said that you went to Lukavica, I think on the 15th of May, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still live in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to the time period prior to May 1995 after you left Sarajevo, dealing with what you said yesterday at transcript page 31046 and 31047, that the transmission lines Sokolac-Vogosca was not repaired and that you being the Bosnian Serb side were forced to connect the transmission line Poljine-Pale so that you could get electricity from Visegrad to Vogosca; is that right? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I even wrote that. We fixed the 110 kV line, and we also repaired the line leading to Poljine, but from Poljine to Sarajevo 4 transformer station at Vogosca we never managed to repair that. That is why we built one and a half kilometres on wooden pillars, and we switched it to 35 voltage and thereby supplied Vogosca and parts of Ilijas with the electricity from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this transition line was installed and put into operation at Pretis, yes?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pretis tasked the Vogosca municipality, and parts of Vogosca municipality had power supply.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This -- this transformer that you -- that you installed was put into operation at Pretis; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if Pretis was in operation or not. That was beyond my remit. I never went to either Pretis factory for the TAS factory. I just passed by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The exhibit that was tendered through you yesterday, D02545, the 15th of September, 1993, document which was signed by you, doesn't that state that the transformer was installed and put into operation at Pretis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show him the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: D02545, Your Honour -- Mr. Registrar [sic].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Then I have one final question -- area for you, Mr. Lubura.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see this document. I signed it at the request of the Executive Committee of the Serbian municipality of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says that there's now 110 -- is the pipeline from Pale to Pretis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Sokolac-Vogosca transmission line. It's not 110, but we switched it to 35 voltage and you can see from this letter that we installed --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Installed what?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A transformer. 8 MVA transformer which was insufficient for this area, but nevertheless it was beneficial for the population of Vogosca and parts of Ilijas to have a continuous energy supply. The needs were much higher, but this was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, you said on page 13 at paragraph 13 of your statement that the Serbs were prepared to transmit energy from Lukavica, Sarajevo 20 that is, to the substations in Dobrinja, Otoka and Skenderija. But you said that the Muslims showed no interest in this proposal. Are you saying that the Muslim side never agreed to repairing the lines feeding these substations should be a priority?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made this proposal to Mr. Durmic at the meetings that we had, but it never materialised. And I have to say that two times 110 Lukavica-Skenderija transmission line hasn't been repaired to this date. It is still inoperational. The rest were fixed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we very quickly see 24265. This is the -- this is the meeting at the Sarajevo airport on the 7th of July, 1994. And if we go down it says both sides agreed -- if we can go further down the page. Onto the next page. That the -- under -- under subparagraph (B). Could we go to the next page, please. I'm sorry, it's on the last page. Under (B) the transmission lines Jablanica-Hadzici-Blazuj and then Blazuj-Famos-Lukavica and Lukavica-Otoka-Nedzarici were agreed on to be a top priority.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answers I said that that was my proposal that Lukavica-Otoka-Nedzarici would be a priority, but it never materialised. This is only the confirmation of my testimony, because as you can see I attended this meeting along with engineers Kulic and Mijatovic, and I proposed that this transmission line be repaired. That was my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But does -- this document does negate the idea that the BiH didn't want to fix it. They wanted it to be a top priority. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no Bosnian side. There are both sides present here. Both parties agreed, and I made this proposal at this meeting to have this transmission line repaired because the southern part of Sarajevo Polje was supplied before the war only from the Famos transformer station, and to that end I made a suggestion to -- to make Lukavica-Otoka-Nedzarici transmission line so that the electricity that arrived at Lukavica station from Mratinje hydro-electric plant in Montenegro be transmitted to the part of Sarajevo under Muslim control. As I said, while I was the manager of transmission this never happened. It was repaired only after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lubura. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I actually would like to have us tender 4265, the last document that was referenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see no problem. Shall we admit it as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As you wish, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 4265 receives number D2548, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, a few questions directly related to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's start with the last. Mr. Lubura, the question put here was whether the Muslims were interested or not in restoring proper supply, and for that purpose I would need D1127, please. While we are waiting, you were shown the document dated 29th of May, 1995, and here's another document of 15 June 1995. I'm going to read it: [In English] "At the very last minute, the Bosnian side this afternoon rejected a proposal to restore utilities to Sarajevo. The Serbian side had agreed to the necessary technical arrangements, arranged by Mr. John Fawcett from the office the special co-ordinator in Sarajevo. But the Bosnian side insisted on UNPROFOR control of Bacevo (Sarajevo's main water pumping station, which is on Serb-controlled territory) as well as ... gas supplies ..." [Interpretation] Item 3 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is re-examination and Mr. Karadzic should be putting a proposition, laying a foundation before he puts a document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do you understand that point, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May the document be taken off the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, if you were in favour of this -- or, rather, were you in favour of having the Muslim side an uninterrupted supply of electricity?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I would have slept soundly if everybody had electricity. I wanted every side or both sides to have as much electricity as possible. However, the technical capacities were such, so we only had 20 plus 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Twenty megawatts plus three for either side?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for them not to receive any power supply -- or, rather, to avoid doing the repair and therefore improve the supply?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that has to do with the technological capacity of transmission lines that were operational. They could not allow any increase. I don't know how many generators were working in Kakanj, so technologically speaking, it was impossible to increase it, because the transformer station in Kiseljak was also supplied from the same source, and they also needed to 20 or 30 megawatts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, because both of you are speaking the same language and which are to be translated into English and French, please speak slowly and put a pause before you start answering the question. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During cross-examination it was suggested to you that the Serbian party intentionally cut off electricity to the Muslim part of Sarajevo. How could this -- this have been achieved? Who did the Serbian side have to ask to have this completed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have to ask me, because I was the manager of the Ilidza plant. Only me and no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you ever received such a request?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't, neither from the military nor from the civilian authorities. Mr. President, I was answerable to the general director of Elektroprivreda of Republika Srpska and his assistant for technical affairs, the manager who was in the head office in Banja Luka, and these were the only people that I reported to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. Today you mentioned that the Muslim side was not interested in a few lines and branches. Do you know that the Muslim side was engaged in sabotaging the provision of utilities?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that we agreed at the Sarajevo airport we tried to put into practice. I said it was my proposal to fix the Lukavica-Otoka-Nedzarici line which was a project that was never implemented. I also know that sometime in the summer of 1995 the Muslims built transformer station in Zovik, and by means of an overhead line they reached Igman, then they installed a 110 kV cable downwards and in my assessment that provided them with about 80 megawatts of electricity from the Jablanica hydro-electric power plant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I show the document now to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Do you have any observations?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the document's dated the 15th of June, 1995, at which time the witness said that he wasn't in Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the point, Mr. Robinson, you raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I made that same point to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm interested in the phenomenon that Mr. Lubura was discussing and that is that the opposing side was sabotaging these attempts and it can shed some more light on the document of 29th of May of that same year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can't have it both ways. That document is already in evidence, and there's no need for you to tender it, but you can just put your case or your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today in cross-examination you were asked a number of questions relating to the requests by the Serbian side for reciprocity -- or, rather, concessions so that something be done for them in order for them to allow something, and reference was made to document P896 in which the Serbian side requested first combat operations to be suspended and then the utilities could be repaired. Why was it necessary to suspend combat operations?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, we couldn't go out into the field if the war was going on. All our technicians would get killed. We needed a cease-fire, and we needed approval from both sides for our crews to go out and repair the transmission lines. I was concerned about the lives and safety of my men, because I didn't have too many of them, and therefore I had to have 100 per cent guarantees by UNPROFOR that there would be no shooting and that we can do our work under such conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Western Bosnia or Republika Srpska or the Banja Luka, Krajina, did they receive power from Jablanica? And was this question ever raised as a matter of reciprocity or a proposal to strike a balance?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in charge only for the Ilidza plant, but since my head office was in Banja Luka, I was aware of their problems, too, and I was personally involved in the building of the so-called Posavski lines through the corridor running between Brcko and Modrica. We built two or three transmission lines in order to have power for Banja Luka from Ugljevik. Banja Luka and Bosanska Krajina as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were in charge of Ilidza, in August of 1992 were you at Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived at Ilidza in August, and I had come from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Muslim side ever shell the water and gas and other supply installations?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the major disruption in the supply of electricity and water for both the Muslim and the Serbian parts of Sarajevo took place in December -- or, rather, the 12th of December when we were shelled from Igman. According to the information that we received over the radio from our electrician on duty, that had been ordered by Juka Prazina. At that time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Lubura.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where did it rise from the cross-examination? And I also note your -- yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was my point, Your Honour. It doesn't arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, during cross-examination it was disputed that the Muslim side sabotaged. It was put that the Serbian side cut off supply intentionally. Page 13, lines 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're talking about supply of electricity, not the shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is separate. It's a separate matter, Mr. Karadzic. Please move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, very well. I will move on. I just wanted to see whether the Serbs indeed did that or was it simply a result of shelling, because shelling causes damage, and we have proof. If you give me one minute, I'll show you D1246.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you already gave evidence yourself. I don't see the point of continuing this way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I dispute the Prosecution position that the Serbs were cutting off supply, whereas we have proof that it was not so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, can you assist us with what aspect of the cross that this would be pertaining to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, Madam Sutherland suggested to the witness that it was the Serbs who intentionally cut off water and electricity supply to the Muslim part of Sarajevo. We have proof, however, that it happened as a result of shelling, that it was not intentional. And it goes directly to what the Prosecution stated and confirms the witnesses words in his statement. On the other hand, on page 13 that we pointed out, it had to do with whether the Muslims wanted to have it fixed or did they sabotage such repairs so as to increase the plight of the inhabitants of Sarajevo. The document speaks to it as well as some other documents we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, we haven't heard evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We haven't heard evidence from this witness at all about the shelling. It's not part of cross-examination, and Mr. Karadzic shouldn't be allowed to re-examine on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But do you agree that it was suggested to the witness that it was the Serbs who had intentionally cut off water and electricity supplies to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The documents that I put to the witness clearly show that. I put that to the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber sees the point of Mr. Karadzic's submissions. We allow the question. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at D1127 briefly, which is two weeks following the document shown by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we dealt with the document. Instead of putting the document, why don't you put the question to the witness directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- with respect, this is something that Mr. Karadzic should have done in his case in chief if he wanted to elicit this sort of information from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In his examination-in-chief, witness said that he was never ordered to cut off the electricity and others, and in your cross-examination it was put to the witness Serbs intentionally cut off electricity and water, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was the summary that Mr. Karadzic was reading out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Para 17 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I put that to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we allow the question suggested by Mr. Karadzic in his previous submission. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have a look at D -- sorry, I put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the reasons for the supply being cut off for Sarajevo. In 1992 you were in Ilidza. You held the position you had in your company. Were there any cases of force majeure? Were there any cases of combat resulting in the cutting off of supplies due to shelling or infantry fighting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I said yesterday that there were two types of failures at -- at transformer stations, the so-called physical failures or failures of the equipment. Physical failures mainly happened due to combat. Lines were destroyed, isolation was destroyed, et cetera. Those were physical failures which required between five and seven days of repair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we next look at D1246. Was there any connection between the supply of water and the supply of electricity?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the water is brought by pumps. I think there were 13 in Bacevo and Komovsi [phoen]. They pumped the water to the central reservoir from which it was distributed to the Mojmilo reservoir supplying the city of Sarajevo. If the transformer station at Blazuj had no electricity, the pumps were not operational, resulting in the fact that there was no water. However, Ilidza didn't have water as well in such cases; in other words, both the Serbs and Muslims were out of water in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read out the first sentence where it says that Ilidza makes the following decision. Who is going to have their water supply cut off due to the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, it's a way of conducting the re-examination in a leading way. I think that's the point you're rising, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, two reasons: For that and also for -- what has the supply of water -- the connection between the supply of water and the supply of electricity got to do with the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you not suggest to the witness that Serbs had cut off electricity and water intentionally?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just instead of putting the document, why don't you lead some foundation before you show the document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have when I asked him whether the supply of water was in any way connected with the supply of electricity, and before that I asked him for the reasons of damage, and this is what this document speaks of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think you did that. You said that after showing the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I would ask the witness if this tallies with his knowledge of the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the 4th of August, I believe. I wasn't there at the time. I arrived in Ilidza on the 15th of August. Mr. Despotovic was the facility manager at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know what the position was of the state leadership vis-a-vis supplying civilians on both sides?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice or thrice I was a member of the delegation headed by deputy prime minister, late Professor Koljevic. I know that he always used to say that we have to make life easier for both sides in the time of war, making sure that they both had enough electricity, water, gas, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look at D104, please. Please cast a look at this directive of mine from March 1993 and tell us whether the gist of the directive is in keeping with what you could observe concerning our position in terms of supply.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This only confirms my testimony. We never intentionally cut off electricity or water unilaterally. Even where repairs were needed, we tried to make things operational as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether the ministries of the RS government undertook certain measures to ensure the supply of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They assisted us. Our basic problem was fuel. Through the government, we received certain amounts of fuel, and UNPROFOR frequently helped in that regard too. As I said, we had to maintain over 250 kilometres of transmission lines. We had fuel expenses, salaries, et cetera, and the government helped us out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have D116.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, is Mr. Karadzic going to put a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has to do with the question I put concerning the ministries and their efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Borivoje Sendic was?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him concerning the Ugljevik-Zvornik transmission line. I believe he was the minister of agriculture with his seat in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. D116, please. Could you read out the title for the Chamber. What was the subject of this meeting? And I was informed about this.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the subject?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Delivery of drinking water to Sarajevo. The date is the 18th of July, 1993. A meeting was held in Pale between the representatives of this ministry and water supply companies in the area of Sarajevo's Serbian municipalities. The topic of the meeting was the supply of drinking water to the part of Sarajevo chiefly populated by Muslims but which also has a large number of Serbian citizens who are practically imprisoned in this city. Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next item, the one pertaining to electricity.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. Electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says the main conclusion, and then we have the supply.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, just below that.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The supply of electricity to pump stations is not continuous; i.e., interruptions in supplying pump stations with electricity are frequent and are chiefly caused by the war operations of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So as not to go on reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was the point I was going to make, Your Honour, about the witness just simply reading out the document which is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Time for you to put a question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does this fit into what you knew about the efforts of the authorities of Republika Srpska to provide supplies to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, all of these documents are positive, favourable; namely, that both electricity and water were regularly sent to the Muslim part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At least you need to pause after the -- until the interpreting is over, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, please, can you read the handwritten part down here where my signature is.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I agree. R. Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Mr. Lubura. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the translation of this document, we do not see who it is that gave his agreement.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I agree," or "in agreement. R. Karadzic," Radovan Karadzic. Your signature; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's not in the translation who it was that gave his agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Usually the signature is not translated, but you have evidence now. Mr. Lubura, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we rise altogether? Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because Ms. Gustafson's taking the next witness so we would need to swap. So perhaps taking an early break would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for half an hour. We'll rise all together. We'll have a break and resume at 10 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radan. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Radan.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give the Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have 1D8609 [as interpreted] in e-court. And I would kindly ask you that we both pause so that the interpreters would accurately interpret what is being said. So please pause before answering my questions. 1D6809. Thank you. Mr. Radan, do you see this statement before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read this statement, and did you sign it then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, I read it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it accurately reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today were your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Fully. They would be absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement as well as the associated documents, package 92 ter. I would like to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, also there are two documents only to be tendered, and we would ask that they be added to our 65 ter list as we didn't have them on our list at the time this witness gave his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have a partial objection to the admission of the statement. In paragraph 8 of the statement there are three documents referenced. The first of those documents is a collection of minutes from local board meetings. That collection of documents has not been tendered, but the first half of that -- of paragraph 8 basically consists of the witness's description of those documents and conclusions about what those documents say. So if the documents themselves aren't being tendered, the witness's description and conclusions in relation to those documents should be redacted, and I know in addition I would not be able to cross-examine the witness on those assertions in any event because those documents are not translated. So I would ask for the first half of paragraph 8 to be redacted. Other than that, there's no objection to the statement. In terms of the associated exhibits, I have no objection to them per se. I note that they are both wrongly described in the statement as minutes of the Novo Sarajevo SDS Municipal Board. In fact, one -- the first document is minutes of a meeting of the Hrasno Brdo local board, and the second is a report from the Nikola Tesla local board. If the Defence is willing to stipulate that the documents are not what they purport to be in the statement, I have no objection to their admission, although I raise it in the event Your Honours would like the accused to clarify that in direct examination with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see 1D6297 briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson said that there's no translation. I was denied access to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's being shown on the screen is actually not the translation of the document that's of the 65 ter number that you asked for.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the translation on the screen is a translation of one of the documents within the 70-page collection but not the first document, which is why the two documents don't match. This is the -- this translation that we see is the document 1D6810, which is being tendered, and uploaded in e-court in terms of translations is only this document, and there are no others. So this document in the collection is untranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I have understood your point with which I agree. So in order for you to tender the statement, including the first half of the -- this paragraph, para 8, you need to lead live with the witness and deal with the 1D6297.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We're not planning to do that, Mr. President, so we can redact the first half of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll admit -- we'll admit the 92 ter statement with the redaction of first half of para 8 as well as the other two associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement document 1D06809 receives number D2549, Your Honours. Document 1D06810 receives number D2550, and document 1D06811 receives number D2551, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'd like to read out the summary of Mr. Radan's statement in the English language: [In English] Branko Radan was born in Topljik, Novo Sarajevo municipality. He served in the Yugoslav People's Army as an ordinary soldier in Nis. Before the war he worked in a number of companies and when the war started he was working as a representative of Ozrenka of Gracanica. He then served as president of the executive authority in Novo Sarajevo municipality. After the multi-party elections he noticed the boundaries between the people of the three nationalities become thicker and deeper. There were already talks about the arming of Muslims and the formation of units as the Green Berets and Patriotic League. He saw groups of young men wearing green berets walking around town and shots fired from infantry weapons were heard in the evening. Unlike the Muslims and Croats, Serbs -- the Serbs were not arming and preparing for war. At the start of the war, Branko Radan was president of the executive authority, Executive Board of Novo Sarajevo municipality. Municipal authorities took the stand that there must not be any discrimination and, in particular, no torture or abuse of the non-Serbian population and security should be guaranteed to all. There was a group of nine Serbian men who created major problems for Muslims and Croats in the area. The executive authority, following several meetings, requested and demanded that the nine men be removed from the Grbavica area by the local police organs. Whatever humanitarian aid arrived in the municipality, it was distributed equally among the different ethnicities in the municipality. Grbavica was shelled from the Muslim side with increasing frequency from Velesici, particularly causing many civilian casualties. Most victims were killed by sniper fire from the Muslim side with positions in Debelo Brdo and tall civilian buildings across the river. For protection against that, the inhabitants of Grbavica used to erect blinds several metres high and made out of blankets in some streets behind which the pedestrians could move unobserved. There were no reprisals against the Muslim civilian population in the municipality. Due to the difficult material situation of the people, the executive authority made use of the humanitarian aid to organise people's kitchen, public kitchen, where the Serbs', Muslims' and Croats' households obtained food without any problem. And that would be the summary, but I would pose few additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, I have a few more questions to put to you in this examination-in-chief. First of all about the SDS and the municipal organs of Novo Sarajevo: Who won the first multi-party election in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: At the first multi-party elections in Novo Sarajevo, SDS won and received most of the votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember what the outcome was for the SDA in that parliament?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I think that it was in third or fourth place in terms of the number of votes obtained.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. I kindly ask you to do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, could you kindly come closer to the microphone so that the interpreters could hear you better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I repeat my last answer? I -- I think that the SDA came third or fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I also kindly ask you to pause before answering my question. Who was the first president of the Municipal Board of the SDS in Novo Sarajevo, and how did this inter-party life function in this Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: When things happen for the first time, as they did in the multi-party elections, very often the president of the Municipal Board changed. The first one was Mr. Savo Lala, then after that, if need be I can tell you, it was Milivoje Savarkapa who was not satisfactory. The name itself says that it's supposed to be a democratic party, the Serb Democratic Party, but there was no democracy. There was no respect. So he was replaced and then Dr. Milivoje --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- came to replace him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters were not able to hear the last one's name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally it was Dr. Milivoje Prijic that was selected as president of the Municipal Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These changes that took place in the Municipal Board, did they take place under some influence from the headquarters of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: The headquarters of the SDS did not interfere, and did not exercise any influence in terms of the elections in our municipality. However, at the proposal of ten boards of the Serb Democratic Party in local communes we asked the leadership headed by President Karadzic to come and attend our session on the 6th of February at the municipality building. This is the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. We wished to present our views and our problems, and we wanted to reach a democratic agreement as to who the officeholder will be, who the president of the Municipal Board of the SDS will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the year was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: 1992, the 6th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At this meeting did I interfere with who it would be, or did I impose what a solution would be to that question? Did I impose any particular name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: You and the other leaders who came with you heard us out at that session, and then in a democratic and conciliatory fashion you recommended that the majority that was in favour of Milivoje Prijic should win and that then Mr. Milivoje Prijic would be the president of the Municipal Board of the SDS; that is to say that you did not interfere at municipal level in this selection of the president of the Municipal Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, was there a Crisis Staff, and if so, when was it established?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was established after the first barricades appeared on the 1st of March, 1992, when the conflict escalated, the conflict among the three sides, or basically between the two sides, the Serb and the Muslim sides. After Gardovic, a member of the wedding party in Bascarsija was killed, barricades were set up, and after these barricades nothing was the same any longer, and it became necessary to organise a Crisis Staff because there was no communication with the seat of the municipality that had been dislocated; that is to say we did not manage to use the resources of the municipal government, and that is why the Crisis Staff was established sometime in mid-March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who headed this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: The first and only president of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo was Mr. Radomir Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What happened with the regular authorities in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo from April until June?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, as for this structure that had been elected after the multi-party elections, the president of the Municipal Board was originally Montenegrin. He went to Montenegro, and it was only the secretary of the municipality, Mr. Mirko Sarovic, who remained in our territory. We had to elect new authorities, and that happened on the 5th of May, 1992, at the recommendation of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was elected?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: As I said, at the recommendation of the president and Crisis Staff, Mr. Danilo Skrba was elected President of the Executive Board. I was the vice-president of the Executive Board, and there were four other persons who were elected as members of the Executive Board, and they were in charge of different matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until the 5th of May, what was the task of the Crisis Staff before the selection?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: It -- in the turbulent situation in Novo Sarajevo and Bosnia-Herzegovina, the task of the Crisis Staff was to prevent the anarchy that seemed to be in the making. The population was supposed to be told that they would be protected in a certain way and effort was to be made to prevent any kind of chaos, and I believe that the Crisis Staff considerably succeeded in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So when were the regular authority organs set up and which ones?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I said I already said that on the 5th of May, 1992, the Executive Committee was established and its task was to gradually undertake the work of the Crisis Staff, which I think basically was also the will of the Crisis Staff. And the Executive Committee did well in assuming those duties so that the Crisis Staff remained operational for only one month, that is to say until the end of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any other changes in the government or authorities and the Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: The first changes took place in July when Mr. Danilo Skrba went to take a new office and at the Assembly session new candidates were proposed for the president of the Executive Committee. I was among the nominees, and then on the 12th of July at the Assembly session, I was elected as president of the Executive Committee. My counter-candidate was Mr. Radomir Neskovic, and after that we set up an Executive Committee that became fully operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone from the leadership try to impose a decision who would be elected president of the Executive Committee? Did anyone try to impose any kind of solutions in that respect?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: At this session we were honoured by the presence of the late Dr. Nikola Koljevic, vice-president of the republic, and Mr. Petko Cancar, the president of the electoral commission, the Commissioner Dragan Djukanovic. And by being present there, they lent importance to the election of the new municipal leadership. I did not notice any other interferences or pressures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if you encountered any security problems in your municipality as of the date when the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I said that we had been trying the whole time to prevent anarchy. That is a normal phenomenon under such circumstances, so we were no exception. We tried in every possible way, because we lived mostly in the urban part of the city with all three ethnic communities. We wanted to protect everybody who remained with us. We had a huge problem with a group that came from outside, meaning that they were not locals. We had problems with them because they were maltreating and harassing our citizens of Muslim and Croat ethnicity. Therefore, we constantly pointed out to these happenings, and at our regular meetings that took place at least once a week, the civilian authorities, the police, and the army underlined, although I was not able to give any tasks to anyone, we made a joint effort to remove those nine persons who were constantly causing problems. And amongst them was Veselin Vlahovic, aka Batko, who was the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These nine persons, did they enjoy any support from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I already said that we could not support these individuals in any way whatsoever, quite the opposite. We did our best to remove them from our territory and prevent them from causing problems, and I think that we managed to do that step-by-step, to remove them from our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they alone or did they have their groups that were gathering around them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, those were groups. Such people easily find followers. There was some kind of vested interest that they had. Whether that was material gain or something else, I don't know, but I don't think that they were doing it for the interest of nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At what time of day did they engage in commission of such acts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, due to the situation that prevailed at the time, a curfew was imposed banning anyone from moving during the night with the exception of police and military police. The civilians were prohibited from moving around, and that was usually the time when they broke the law and this regulation. So they were active during the night when no one was able to prevent them from doing so except the victims themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you personally have any problems with these groups?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, you see, I did have problems. After my idea and my intention became known to engage the police and the army to help us remove them from our municipality, shortly after that in front of the municipal building my car was riddled with bullets. Somebody shot at it in broad daylight, in plain view of the passers-by. After that, the military police arrived, arrested the offender, took him to the prison at Kula, but only a few days after that he was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that they gradually disappeared from the area. Were they interconnected or were they acting independently? Did they disappear group by group?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, they acted independently. Batko was not connected to anyone, not the army or anyone else. He was a freelancer. The one who shot at my car and another one who killed a soldier, father of three, without any reason whatsoever, I'm talking about Mr. Zoran Lackovic, was incarcerated at Kula. But upon his release somebody took revenge on him, whether it was the soldiers or companions of Zoran Lackovic, but they avenged the death of their colleague, and the perpetrator was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you stay in the post of the president of the Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Until the 12th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who succeeded you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I was succeeded by Captain Budimir Obradovic, the deceased Budimir Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Budimir Obradovic wanted to introduce even a higher degree of discipline in our municipality. Since those who did not want discipline and order resented this, in his office in the municipal building, Mr. Budo Obradovic was assassinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you and Mr. Obradovic as executive branch, did you enjoy support among the municipal organs to impose law and order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, we did have support, because regular reports were being received from the ground either from the military organs or through municipal channels. So we had communication, and we enjoyed full support of our intentions and our actions on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In September 1992, was there a significant relocation of the population in Novo Sarajevo municipality, and if so, can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes. On the 30th of September, 1992, in the early morning hours there are some estimates that about 300 Muslim citizens crossed over the bridge on the Vrbanja and went to the territory of the federation -- or, rather, under the control of their forces. Since I wasn't personally present there but I nevertheless reacted immediately by talking to the police and inquired about this incident, I was told that that happened with the inhabitants who were living on the front line in Jevrejsko Groblje, Gornja Kovacici and Donji Kovacici, and on a daily basis there was shooting, fighting, shelling in that area. The Serbian forces were holding defence positions. They had moved their families further back in order to provide safety, but the Muslims stayed in their houses and they were behind the VRS. In order for them to be safer, I don't know who agreed on that or whether they organised themselves, they decided to cross over to the other side. As far as I know, no pressure was exerted. Nothing was done under coercion, and people moved across. So I think that it was an organised move and that it was a satisfactory move, and I have proof in the incident that took place on the 15th of November when 15 buses of Serbs crossed across -- passed across our territory and went to Belgrade. So there was some kind of goodwill there, and there was a response from our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Muslim civilians living along the confrontation line, did they have any other alternative to be safe? What could they have done?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, they could have withdrawn, but believe me, Grbavica was fully packed with refugees. All the vacant premises were filled by people, flats and all other residential areas. So there was very little possibility to provide shelter elsewhere for those people living on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any Muslims remain at Grbavica, those who weren't living along the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes. According to some estimates, between 3 -- 1.350 and 1.500 inhabitants remained, and they enjoyed all the same rights in terms of humanitarian aid, medical assistance and security. We tried to provide identical conditions for them as the ones accorded to the Serbs and Croats. So as I said, between 1.350 and 1.500 of them remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they stay there until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, until reintegration took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that they were treated in an equal manner. How were they treated with in terms of acquired rights; for example, the rights to a pension?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, following my election in June of 1992 as the president of the Executive Committee, I immediately launched an initiative to gather reliable information about the rights acquired prior to the war. So anyone who was able to prove that they were entitled to a pension, whether they were Muslims, Serbs, or Croats, could provide such certificates and they were eligible to receive pension. So there was no discrimination against anyone in that respect. That also applied to medical services, distribution of humanitarian aid, soup kitchens. Just like everybody else, they were entitled to receive aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What would happen if a retired person did not submit the necessary documents in time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: All those who failed to provide proper documents and information in time regarding their rights to pension could enjoy this, and they would receive back pay for the period that they were delayed, and they were on equal footing as the others who applied in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did humanitarian aid cross the territory of your municipality, the one directed to the Muslim part?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, that was one of the way to cross it, because the road on Trebevic was closed. Humanitarian aid was delivered on a regular basis and in the quantities required, and there were no disturbances in that manner. In May there was a humanitarian aid convoy of some eight tractor trailers, and the esteemed cardinal Veljko Peulic [as interpreted] was in the delegation escorting these convoys, and they crossed over to the other territory without any problems. So there was other convoys escorted by Colonel Zarkovic, who was our liaison officer with UNPROFOR, and they ensured that they would reach their destination securely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think you said cardinal Vinko Peulic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did at any point the humanitarian aid delivery became obstructed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, that became most prominent before some major holidays. Everyone who had anyone in Sarajevo wanted to send some stuff that would help people to celebrate their holidays, and this usually happened in November, December, and January, and I'm talking about the end of 1992 and beginning of 1993 when the humanitarian aid reached Lukavica, but the Muslim forces did not give them permission to pass through Sarajevo. After several pleas, we had to unload this stuff in the warehouse of Energoinvest, and when the permission was granted, it was sent to Sarajevo. However, this permission was never given, and it stayed there until January for three months and it went off, most of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there any attempt on the part of the population of Grbavica, non-Serb population and Muslims, to cross to the other side?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes. They thought that they could reunite with their families and have better living conditions, but there were no expulsions carried out by us. All of this was done by so-called freelancers who wanted to help both sides and help people to get across to the other territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the term "slobadni strelci" can be translated as "freelance" person. What do you mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Usually such people had ham radio stations, usually taxi drivers who could communicate with the other side, who could establish contact, and then they made agreements to have one-for-one exchanges or to try and entertain the requests of one or the other side. It was not done in an organised fashion. That is why I called those people freelance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions at this point, your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radan, as you have noted, most of your evidence was admitted in writing, i.e., your statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Gustafson. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and just to alert the Chamber, I will do my best to move as efficiently as I can. I estimated an hour for this witness.
