I've been given 45 minutes, but since my estimate, I -- there has been substantial new information elicited by the accused, and had I known that, my estimate would have been longer. Like I said, I will do my best, but I alert the Chamber now I may need to ask for some additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Duly noted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radan. Just to get the chronology of your positions clear, you became president of the Novo Sarajevo Executive Board in July 1992. Prior to that I understand you were the vice-president of the Executive Board, and you became vice-president in May 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, on the 5th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And prior to that appointment in May of 1992, is it correct that you had no official position in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: You are correct. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And Dr. Milivoje Prijic, he was the president of Novo Sarajevo municipality during the same period of time that you were president of the Executive Board; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 7 of your statement, you said that: "Unlike the Muslims and Croats, the Serbs were not preparing for war because they were convinced that they will remain in the federal state of Yugoslavia, where for them peace was guaranteed." By the term "preparing for war," were you referring to activities such as arming or preparing armed units for their engagement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes. Preparing armed units for conflict. Much earlier than anyone else, the Muslims organised themselves in the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, whereas the Serb side was doing nothing in that respect at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Radan does not have a hard copy of his statement before him, perhaps it may be of assistance if I provided him with one, and Ms. Gustafson can carry on more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have your statement with you, Mr. Radan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I was told that the rules would not allow that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, just in relation to your last answer, the Chamber has received evidence that at a meeting in December 1991, Mr. Karadzic distributed secret instructions for the organisation and operation of the organs of the Serbian people in emergency conditions to municipal SDS officials, and I refer to the evidence P5 and P2568 at transcript page 16656. And the stated purpose for issuing those instructions was the suspicion that Bosnia would be taken out of Yugoslavia, and that's page 1 of P5. Now, you said that the Serbs were convinced that they would remain in Yugoslavia, and that is why they weren't preparing for war. Were you aware at the time that the SDS leadership issued these instructions in December of 1991 to municipal SDS authorities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: I became a member of the Municipal Board or the local commune board in the Vraca local commune in December 1991. Up until that time, I received all information from the media. In other words, I was not active in the work of the party, and I was not able to get by these -- this information that you referred to. Everything I learned was learned through following Assembly sessions, public addresses and communiques from both -- from all sides. At the time, I interpreted such information in my own way. I was in no position to hear about these instructions issued by Mr. Karadzic provided to the local boards.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a reference? Where does it say that I had them distributed?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I provided that reference. It was P2568 at transcript page 16656.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It don't say that I distributed it by hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If it doesn't, then I apologise. If it was distributed at a meeting chaired by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, you stated earlier in your evidence that the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff was formed in mid-March 1992. Were you -- I take it, then, you were unaware that there was an earlier Crisis Staff formed in your municipality pursuant to these December 1991 instructions, and I refer there to P2575.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I wasn't familiar with that. I know what happened after the barricades in March because I heard about it at the time. I knew there was the president of the Crisis Staff who was Mr. Neskovic, and I wasn't aware of who the other members are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to Ms. Gustafson. In the last line, it says indeed what she claims to have said, but it was put that way by a witness. The last line reads that the witness indeed said that I had it distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I thank the accused for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, so if you were unaware of the creation of this Crisis Staff, I take it you were also not aware that at the meeting in December 1991 where that Crisis Staff -- Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff staff was established, that Drago Kovac, Milenko Jovanovic, and Momir Garic, representatives of civilian protection, the MUP and the TO were tasked with item 9 of those instructions which was an instruction to prepare an estimate of the number of necessary active and reserve policemen, TO units, and civilian protection units. And on that basis bring them up to full manpower levels and take any other necessary action for their engagement in keeping with the developments. An order to activate these units shall be issued by the Crisis Staff in the municipality. I take it you were not aware that those three individuals were given that task.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I knew all three of them. As for their specific duties, I wasn't aware of that nor do I know what the results were of the things they were supposed to undertake. In the territory of our part of the municipality where I resided, I did not feel the effects of those developments. We were not preparing ourselves, as I have said before. At least I had no part in any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You may not have had a part in any such thing, but you agree, do you not, that bringing police, TO, and civilian protection units up to full manpower levels and taking any other necessary action for their engagement is a preparation for war, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: In the overall situation, the Serb people did not prepare themselves for war but for defence in order to remain part of Yugoslavia and to defend themselves by pre-empting any possible developments similar to those from World War II. They were acting based on their experience. If you want to invoke the meeting and instructions from 1991 and the three people in question and their tasks, perhaps I could say that I would have taken part if someone had offered it to me. I saw through my own experience what the members of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets were doing around Sarajevo. Out of prevention and out of fear, I would have definitely joined the defence efforts in order to defend what was ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. The Chamber also heard evidence from Mr. Garic who testified for the Defence that Mr. Garic was in contact with Colonel Gagovic, the assistant commander for logistics of the JNA 4th Corps, to obtain weapons. Do you know anything about Mr. Garic's efforts to obtain weapons from the JNA in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know which period this statement by Mr. Garic refers to. I did not take part in it. I do know Mr. Garic, but as of the beginning of the conflict, I don't know what he had been doing before that, and I told you that I was unaware and unfamiliar with the tasks he and the two other men were apparently assigned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. Thank you. I'd like to move on now to talk about the Serbian nine men that you refer to in your statement who were causing problems by mistreating Croats and Serbs [sic] in the municipality. You refer to this at paragraph 13 of your statement. You said that you knew these nine men by name, but you had only mentioned Batko or Veselin Vlahovic in your evidence. Can you name the other nine men you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: During that time I only knew of this nickname Batko. As for the other eight, Zorka Cepter, this and that, they had all sorts of nicknames, but I never obtained their particulars. When I mentioned the meeting with the police and military in order to have something done about it, I mentioned only their nicknames, and yet everyone knew who they were. Neither then nor now I know -- do I know their first and last names, because they do not hail from our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So the police and the army knew more about these men than you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I suppose as much. Whenever there was an Assembly session, someone from the police reported on their activities, what they did, where -- what proceedings they instituted, et cetera, and they always kept going back to the topic of security. In the reports they would submit figures. This is how many people we have criminally prosecuted, et cetera. However, the figures came without the names. I suppose they had appropriate information and they had more of it because it was their job to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said this was a problem -- this problem with the Serbian nine men. I understand you said this was a problem from the start of the war. When did you first become aware of this -- the crimes committed by this group?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: It wasn't continuous but sporadic, whenever someone had the chance to do something. Such things did not reach me directly as the President of the Executive Board. I suppose that citizens reported incidents to the police and the police had such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you to listen carefully to my questions and try to answer them as precisely as possible. The question was simply when you first became aware, by whatever means, of Batko's crimes and these nine men.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the question. I heard about his acts in July 1992 at a funeral. A cousin of mine who had been a fighter was buried on that occasion, Zoran Vitkovic. Batko came there, among others, and boasted his activities. It was along the lines of ridicule. So that was in early July 1992. That's when the funeral was and that's when I heard of Batko for the first time. I did not know him before that. He was not part of any unit. He was not at the front lines. He was just being a maverick.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But he wore a military uniform; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Even those who were not in the army wore uniforms so as not to be drafted. It was calling cards to -- to try and be seen as someone who was already engaged in the military, but it was no guarantee of anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So I take it you -- your answer's affirmative, that Batko wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You first heard about his acts in July 1992, and then you said earlier today that you constantly pointed out these happenings at weekly meetings with the police and the army. So you began pointing out the crimes of this group sometime after you became aware of them in July at these weekly meetings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you also said earlier today that at one point Batko was arrested after he shot at you in your car. When was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I didn't say Batko fired on that occasion. It was Zoran, aka Zoka. It wasn't Batko who fired at my car. It was Zoran, also known as Zoka. He shot at my car. Never in my statement did I say it was done by Batko.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But Zoka was one of these nine men you refer to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when did that happen? When was your car shot at by Zoka?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Just following the period where these appeals were being made to have them removed from the municipality, which was some time in September in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So in September of 1992, these nine men were still committing crimes in the municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: By that time there were fewer of them, because one or two of them were no longer in our municipality. So we went down from the number of nine. In stages there were fewer and fewer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Was Batko still committing crimes in Novo Sarajevo in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I think by virtue of his presence alone, well, it's a particular kind of personality who couldn't do without terrorising and mistreating others. I suppose, well, because it was not within my remit to go about following him, I forwarded information to the police presuming that they would do their job, and I suppose they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So Batko was still present in the municipality in September 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that after your car was shot at, that Zoka was taken to Kula and then released after a few days. Do you know who released Zoka from Kula?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Believe me when I say I don't. An authorised official must have released him, but I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness be asked to either approach the microphones or speak up.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You've been asked to move closer to the microphone so that the interpreters can hear you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I was facing you, that's why. Thank you. Do I need to repeat?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. I think -- I think your answer was heard. So -- but Kula was a regular prison, and it was run by the Ministry of Justice under Momcilo Mandic; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So earlier when you said that the nine men didn't have any support from the authorities, one of these men obviously had some -- some support from the authorities, in particular some authorised person, as you put it, who released him from Kula; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I suppose that the legal formalities were done. They were interviewed, et cetera, in order to establish what they had done. Now, what the police actually did I'd rather not go into. It's matter for the judiciary and the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. The Chamber has received evidence that the Novo Sarajevo police were well aware of Batko's crimes in May of 1992, and that's P6017. Do you have any reason to dispute that information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: No. By nature, I am a legalist. I abide by the law, and I believe there were other people who were more competent to deal with it. I did not assign myself any right to judge their work. I was not neither present nor competent to assess that. I suppose they worked diligently and in the best manner they knew how.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You suppose they worked diligently. The MUP special forces were based in Novo Sarajevo, in Vraca; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, in the police school, the police academy.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And there was a significant army presence in your municipality, including the SRK corps command at Lukavica, a battalion command in Grbavica, and troops stationed throughout your municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, given this substantial police and army presence and accepting that the police were aware of Batko's group committing crimes beginning in May of 1992, and your evidence that Batko was still in the municipality in September of 1992, it's clear, is it not, that the police and the army could have stopped Batko's crimes long before his eventual removal from the municipality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I agree something could have been done earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the reason nothing was done earlier about Batko was because Batko was being protected by the Bosnian Serb leadership; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I was part of that leadership, and I expressed my opinion, and I stand by it. One cannot make such brushstroke remarks and say that the Serb leadership was protecting Batko.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to turn now to 65 ter 18857A, please. We're about to look at an extract from a book written by Biljana Plavsic. You're familiar with Mrs. Plavsic; right? She was a member of the Presidency at the time.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, in fact, up until the beginning of the war she lived in November Sarajevo, in Grbavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the rest of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could you just repeat your last answer for the interpreters, Mr. Radan.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Biljana Plavsic lived in Grbavica in a neighbourhood called Soping.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go to the next page in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S, please. Mr. Radan, I'd like to direct your attention to the bottom right-hand corner of the document in B/C/S. It's the second paragraph that starts just about halfway down the page where Mrs. Plavsic describes how she had a meeting with the UN High Representative for Refugees in Lukavica in July 1992. And this is at the top of the English. And she describes how she is stopped at the intersection for the roads Trebevic, Grbavica, and Lukavica. About halfway down that passage, in fact, right at the bottom of the screen in the B/C/S, she says: "A group of people waved at me and I got out of the car. They got to the point immediately." If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S: "I expected them to request something for themselves, but they had another issue. They were talking about the events at Grbavica, and they were Serbs. According to them, it was dangerous for the non-Serbs to live in that part of the city. They told me that certain Batko and several people of his kind were forcibly entering the Croatian and Muslim apartments at night and taking the men away. Some of these men have not been seen after this event. They were looting and blackmailing the people. The Serbs who opposed this became a target of this maniac and his group." Now, that's more or less an accurate description of what Batko was up to at the time in Grbavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, you see, I would just like to ask -- well, I know roughly when the book was published and I know who the author of the book is, and I know for what purpose it was written. Nothing is in dispute there. This that is written here, that's something I've often said myself. But for these allegations to be made by Ms. Biljana Plavsic after so many years, she was in our territory most of the time, and I don't know what she did in order to help us to eradicate this evil that did exist in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to now direct your attention to a further extract beginning approximately nine lines down from where we just finished reading, and this is at the bottom of the English where she says: "If half of what the people at the crossroad told me is true, then this is horrible. In that case, then the local authorities have failed." And then she describes how she went to the municipality building and she said: "The president of the municipality was not there but it did not matter because the other quickly gathered. I told them why I had come and asked them whether it was possible that such evil-doings were being tolerated. They were silent." And if we go to the next page in the English, a few lines down she says: "I asked him who Batko was. At the mention of that name, they even got scared. I came to a conclusion that those men were completely unable to cope with the situation and they were the ones representing the authorities. I got the feeling that those people had earlier been some small potatoes in the local communities, and I was not wrong. I asked them who their municipal president was." Sorry, if we could now go to the next half of the page in B/C/S. Thank you: "They mentioned his name. He is a doctor trading in medicines and representing a company. He is a Montenegrin. I did not achieve anything there at the municipality building, but the fact that a member of the Presidency was informed about the events which they were obviously trying to hide must have had some effect. I would immediately inform the Presidency and ask that someone should take responsibility, and that was exactly what I did." Mr. Radan, were you present at this meeting with Mrs. Plavsic when she came to the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: No, I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when she describes the president of the municipality as being a Montenegrin doctor trading in medicines, that's a description of Dr. Prijic who is municipal president at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes. He was born in Montenegro, but he lived and worked in Sarajevo. He was the director of the Galenika representative office in Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Okay. And if we could go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last extract from this which is on the next page in the English, and it's on page 5 of the B/C/S. And it's on the left-hand side of the B/C/S page, beginning in the first full paragraph, about four lines down where she says after her meeting with Ogata in Lukavica she dashed off at great speed to Pale to attempt to prevent the activity of the mad Batko. She says: "I entered one of the rooms in Kikinda where I find all the relevant persons for solving this problem. Radovan is there; Momo, Momcilo Mandic, justice minister; Mico Stanisic, police minister. I didn't even mention to them the conversation I had had with Ogata but straight away moved to the events at Grbavica. I expect wonder, worry, astonishment but there is none of it. Momcilo Mandic smirked, that is the proper term for his face at the moment, and said, 'Oh, Batko,' so to the interior minister as if we were talking about some playful child and his games. Therefore they are familiar with the men and his activities. They know him very well and they do not hide it. So these are his protecters and the ones giving him orders, as Zoran Vitkovic mentioned. I told them that I thought they were unfamiliar with such occurrences and with that person and so had intended to have them issue a warrant to arrest him," and then there's a quote, "'but now I see you are familiar with everything and I now ask the Presidency that the two of you be arrested.' I addressed Karadzic as the president of the Presidency and sought that these two ministers be arrested or that they resign immediately." And then she describes how she's been harassed by Momcilo Mandic since then, and a few lines down she says: "Radovan's reply to my request for the resignation of these ministers reiterated a number of times was always, 'You are asking me to cut off my right arm.'" Now, that explain why Batko and his group were able to operate with impunity for so many months in Grbavica despite the significant police and army presence in the municipality, doesn't it, Mr. Radan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, you see, this is how I would answer: This book was written by Mr. Rajko Vasic. I don't know what he wrote before that. This information and these references to Zoran Vitkovic's statements, a young man who was killed in July 1992, and I spoke about that funeral when I first heard of these wrong-doings. That was the funeral of Zoran Vitkovic. This same Zoran Vitkovic at the request of Biljana Plavsic, with eight or nine of his men, when the fiercest fighting was taking place in Grbavica, upon instructions from Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, from the 9th or 10th floor of a building, he carried Biljana Plavsic's 85-year-old mother downstairs. So I don't know how relevant these statements are in view of this time distance, and with all due respect to the late Zoran Vitkovic, this relevant information taking into account what he said and not taking into account what somebody from the municipality says, an elected official. So she took another route. She took the wrong route. She didn't do things right. As for all of this that she says about this meeting in Kikinda, I was not present, so I cannot say anything about that. So this speaks of Biljana and her testimony and what she spoke of afterwards and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You say you don't know how relevant these statements are in view of this time distance. This book was written in 2005, admittedly some years these events, but you're testifying about these events in 2012. So if we're to accept your words in 2012 about what happened, there's no reason we can't accept Ms. Plavsic's words in 2005; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: This book had a completely different purpose, completely different. The writing of Ratko Vasic had a completely different purpose. I am just testifying to you about situations when I was present. Now, if this book was written in 2005, the late Zoran Vitkovic was killed in the war in Kotorac in 1992, and now all of a sudden to refer to statements made by the late Zoran Vitkovic and not to take into account statements of persons who were relevant and alive in that period, I don't know what purpose that can serve. As for all the situations when I was present, when I could do something, I did do something.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that extract, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. He hasn't confirmed anything about the last portion of the extract involving the meeting with Dr. Karadzic, nor could he have been expected to. So to that extent, I think it's -- that portion of it's inadmissible beside the fact that it's a third party's statement many years after the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, of course there's no bar to hearsay at this Tribunal and there is certainly no bar to having extracts of books submitted. It's happened in this trial in the past, and I point in particular to Mr. Karadzic's tendering extracts of Lord Owen's book through Prosecution witnesses. And in any event, whether or not the witness has confirmed this is not relevant. He stated that Batko wasn't protected or connected to anyone, and this is direct impeachment of that. Apart from that, much of what is in this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I stated. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We are having a debate among the parties. Please --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in any event, much of what the -- much of what is in this extract has in fact been confirmed by the testimony of the witness. So the -- the extract certainly meets the standards for reliability and probative value under Rule 89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you were not with us yesterday, but I reiterated the Chamber's prior practice with respect to third-party statements in which you usually admit the third-party statement when it is to be confirmed by the witness or commented upon. So what would be the reason for you to tender or to admit this part of Mrs. Plavsic's book?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Impeachment, Your Honours, and I don't think there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What point of testimony is this going to impeach? What part of Mr. Radan's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radan denied that Batko was being protected by the leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which includes himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider this issue together with Tintor's interview and give its ruling on Tuesday together.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radan, you referred in your earlier evidence to the fact that the situation with crime improved over time. It is the case, though, is it not that many months after the events that you talked about with Batko, in particular in November of 1992, there was still a problem of massive crime being committed on a massive scale in Novo Sarajevo, in particular by members of the military; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, you were there. Was there --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Which massive crimes?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in particular, mistreatment of the non-Serb population, harassment, rape, physical mistreatment, and robbery.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Had I known about that, I would have reported it to the police. As I said in the previous case, I was in a position to ensure conditions, living conditions, that were sort of adequate, but there was the civilian police, there was the military police that was supposed to do their job. I tried to protect people in my own neighbourhood as much as I could when I knew about things.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to cut you off. My time is very limited. You did answer my question. You said, "I don't know about that."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have P5065, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a document that's in fact referenced in your statement in support of your claim about the number of people killed by sniper fire from the Muslim side. It's the minutes of a 15 November 1992 meeting between SRK commanders and municipality presidents and attended by General Mladic as well. And if we could go to page 2 in the English, staying on page 1 in the B/C/S. You can see that your name is listed as -- you're listed as being present under number 23. You were present at this meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to page 4 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. This is part of the introduction by General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have page 3 in the B/C/S. Sorry, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And there are a number of points about halfway down the page under the heading "Flaws," and about halfway down he lists "genocide on other nations" as one of the flaws. If we could now go to page 9 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S. This is now Colonel Lugonja speaking, who was the chief of security in the SRK command, and at the top of the English and about half way down in the B/C/S, he says: "Extremely widespread theft, robbery, violence and other crimes. Everything has been stolen," et cetera. And then under the next point, he says: "The understanding and practice of individuals and groups that they are masters of life and death to every individual of different ethnicity resulting in cases of unnecessary mistreatment and killing of members of other ethnicities, especially Muslims. Such people see the Geneva and other conventions as obsolete and unnecessary in this war. If we could go to the bottom of the page in English and the next page in the B/C/S. And this is still Colonel Lugonja speaking. And he refers, under the fourth point in B/C/S, near the bottom of the English, he refers to widespread theft, robbery, and all forms of violent behaviour, intensive war profiteering. And under the next point, nearly total financial and legal insecurity particularly in specific areas Grbavica, et cetera. Widespread belief that the war provides an opportunity to profit as much as possible. And if we could go to page 12 of the English and page 9 of the B/C/S. This is Dr. Prijic speaking, the president of Novo Sarajevo municipality. And this is near the bottom in the B/C/S, near the top in the English. Sorry, near the middle in the English. And he says that there are some problems involving robberies and shootings by various soldiers. The army's assistance and intervention in the prevention of problematic actions would be of great benefit. And in the next paragraph he says the soldiers' morale in Novo Sarajevo So is falling. A great portions of soldiers is exercising unruly behaviour. Mass removals of property from the municipality, rape, expulsions from flats are going unpunished affecting morale. And then he says the military police are consolidated but still not strong enough. You were there when Dr. Prijic reported this to the SRK command and that soldiers were committing mass crime in municipality, and that was the reality at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't massive. In order to make things as serious as possible because it was such a eminent gathering, the late President Prijic put things in very serious terms, more serious than was actually the case, but it is true that such things did exist. That's why we took all the measures that we did. However, he presented this before the top echelons of the military. He presented this problem which was evident.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, it's also clear from General Galic's reference to the flaw of the genocide on other nations and to Colonel Lugonja's reference to extremely widespread theft, robbery, violence, and other crimes, and the reference to the understanding and practice of individuals and groups that they are masters of life and death to every individual of different ethnicity, that there was indeed a significant level of crime against non-Serbs at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, all of that we did point out. We said that all of this was happening, but classifying it as genocide, I think that that is not right, because it is well known what genocide means according to these formulations. So I accept all the rest, that that kind of thing happened, except for this formulation, that it was genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson -- Ms. Gustafson, we'll have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Number one, I would like to know how long she plans to be so we can try to plan our next witness; and, secondly, Mr. President, I would ask that we adopt a practice that you had with Dr. Karadzic when it came to additional time for cross-examination, and that is to ask the Prosecution how much it needs and then to give them a specific amount of time so that we can equalise the playing field on which both parties have had to operate on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm keeping a close eye on this. And then I also noted, as Ms. Gustafson indicated, Mr. Karadzic raised some additional things in his chief examination. That's why I'm -- we are allowing some more time to Ms. Gustafson, but fair enough to ask how much longer she would need.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I am almost finished with this topic. I have two further topics which are the ones that were raised new today, and it should take me about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break and resume at 20 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, just before the break, I had asked you whether there was indeed a significant level of crime against non-Serbs at the time of this document we looked at here which was November 1992, and you said, Well, all of that we did point out. We said all of this was happening. Earlier in respect to a question that Mr. Karadzic put to you about whether there was any attempt on the part of the population of Grbavica, the non-Serb population, to cross to the other side, you said, "Yes. They thought they could reunite with their families and have better living conditions, but there were no expulsions carried out by us." It's true, is it not, that one of the reasons that non-Serbs were fleeing or attempting to flee the municipality or leaving the municipality was their flight or attempted flight from the significant level of crime against non-Serbs in Grbavica by members of the military as described in this report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I officially don't know about a single incident in which this was cited as the reason for crossing over, but I also know that there was ethnic divisions. Not expulsions, but divisions along ethnic lines. I mentioned the 15th of November, 1992, when 300 people left from our municipality and then again 15 buses of Serbs, or maybe people of other ethnicities as well, crossed over into Serbia. So the people wanted to have a choice and to go and live together with their compatriots. It is possible, though, that the reasons that you mentioned did exist, that people were being subjected to harassment, that they were seeking a way to cross over in order to escape such situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like now to turn page 26 of the English and page 18 of the B/C/S in this document. And we have seen earlier, Mr. Radan, Mr. Prijic -- or Dr. Prijic mentioning the need to strengthen the military police and asking for the army's assistance with the problems of crime, and here we see these are concluding remarks by General Mladic, and in the middle of the page in both the English and B/C/S there's an entry where he says: "Co-operation with SRJ, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, is good, but our entrepreneurs should be called to account, municipality presidents should put an end to the robberies." In your assessment did municipality presidents have the means and authority to put an end to large-scale crime by VRS soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I said earlier that neither the president of the municipality nor the president of the Executive Council had any leverage to -- to do that despite having the will and the desire to do so. They weren't able to secure normal life, and they didn't have instruments to put that into practice without co-operation with the army, the civilian police, and the military police. Our recommendations and pleas with regard to what has to be done in the form of joint co-operation among all parties concerned was the only way and our only option.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn now to a topic that was raised by Dr. Karadzic this morning about the departure of some Muslims from the area of are Kovacici. And actually you mentioned it again a moment ago, and I'd just like to clarify, because I think you gave two different dates. What was the date that this departure took place?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid there is an error in interpretation. The witness said on the 30th September Muslims and then Serbs in November, but although I refrained from intervening, this is what the transcript reads.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, what was the date that these Muslims departed, these Muslims from Kovacici?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: The Muslims left on the 30th of September, 1992, in the early morning hours of that day. Possibly the other party was alerted about their arrival, because on the other side of the Vrbanja, there were already journalists and cameras and crews, and this information reached east river in New York within 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So -- and you said that they were living along the confrontation line where there was shooting on a daily basis, and you cited that as the reason for them to leave. That confrontation line was established in April of 1992, and it didn't -- it remained static throughout this period; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: No. It never shifted in that specific area.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you said earlier that there was daily fighting in that area, and yet for a reason that you apparently aren't aware of, for some reason after living on the confrontation line where there was daily fighting for about six months, all of a sudden in a single day 300 Muslims decided to up and leave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, whatever was going on with the Muslims -- and, sorry, Kovacici, that's a different area than Grbavica. Those are two different neighbourhoods in Novo Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: No, they are not. There's Vrbanja Most, Kovacici, Grbavica 1 and Grbavica 2, and Hrasno. This is how these local communities are situated, but they constitute one whole. Then you have the Jewish Cemetery, Grbavica 1, Grbavica 2, which is on the left river of the Miljacka downstream from the Vrbanja.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 09390G, please. And if we could zoom in on the -- basically the middle of this map. A little bit more. A little bit more, please. And if we could shift the map up. And zoom in again. And that should be fine there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radan, can you see the word "Kovacici" on this map? Right about in the middle of the screen.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that depicts the neighbourhood of Kovacici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like -- I'm going to ask you to put a circle around that, and the usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And immediately to the left of Kovacici is the Jewish Cemetery; right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: If viewed from here, then it's between Kovacici and Souk Bunar. That's where the Jewish Cemetery is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you mark the Jewish Cemetery with a J.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you see the word "Grbavica" to the left, on the left-hand side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That depicts the neighbourhood of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And could you draw a circle around that, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, these are clearly two different neighbourhoods aren't they, Mr. Radan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: No. It's one whole. This is Grbavica 2, which I encircled, and then between Kovacici and Grbavica 2 you have Grbavica 1. So all these neighbourhoods are interconnected.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, they may be linked, but they're two different neighbourhoods, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: No, that's the settlement of Grbavica. All of that belongs to Grbavica. It may be called Kovacici, Grbavica 1, Grbavica 2. These are all interconnected to constitute one whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that. Whatever was happening to these Muslims in Kovacici that you referred to on the 30th of September, it is the fact, is it not, that hundreds of Muslims were expelled from Grbavica on the 30th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I don't know on what basis you have established that to be a fact, because that's not what I've said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you a document, but before we do that, if you could please initial this map in the bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to tender that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For clarity, why don't we ask the witness to circle the Grbavica 1 as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you able to circle Grbavica 1, Mr. Radan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you write down G1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Today is 6th of December, 2012.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit that as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document marked by the witness becomes Exhibit P6036, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could have P1266 on the screen. Sorry, P1266. I don't believe this is P1266. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm sorry. I did see this one. Yes, I did see it. When I came here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So the Defence showed this document to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what did they ask you about this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: They asked me about what I knew with regard to this document, and that's what I testified here. Only one correction, small correction. It says here Bristol Hotel, whereas the people crossed to the other side across the Vrbanja Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And all this information that you received about what happened to the Muslims on this day you testified earlier you -- you received that information from the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: No. I said that I learned about this and then I officially inquired with the police what information they had, because they were the ones who were supposed to provide official information. One should not rely on hearsay and rumours. That's why I requested official information.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier in response to a question by the accused you said: "Since I wasn't personally present there, I nevertheless reacted immediately by talking to the police." So if you didn't find out about this from the police, who did you find out about it from given that you weren't personally there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: People were talking inside and outside the municipal building when I arrived at work at around 8.30. When I arrived in my office, I rang the police in order to find out what actually happened. After that, after I received this information, I took my car and drove to Pale to talk to Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, the speaker of the Assembly, and to find out if he knew anything about this. He was completely astounded, because he didn't have accurate information. And then later on it was found out that this whole thing was something that was self-organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, it's time to come to your last point.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you said people were talking inside and outside the municipal building. You said later on you found out that -- later on you found out that this whole thing was something that was self-organised. So in the morning that you arrived at the municipal building, were people talking about the fact that Muslims were being expelled?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I said outside the building, and when I was arriving, I heard about it on my way to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I asked you whether people were talking about the fact that Muslims were being expelled. Is that what you heard outside the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: They didn't make any assertions. They were just claiming to know that they crossed over to the other side and that they heard this information. There were individuals, though, who claimed that they had been expelled, but since I did not want to rely on unconfirmed information, I resorted to contacting official sources to hear from them what actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radan, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while we still have this document on the screen, Mr. Radan, tell me, did you know any of the persons mentioned in this document, for example this liaison officer of the BH Army who was in charge of liaising with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This -- first of all, it's clear that this document was shown to the witness in proofing. The accused elected not to discuss it with the witness in his testimony. I didn't ask him anything about the individuals who drafted this report. This is not proper redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would disagree. I think she can't expect to show a report to a witness and ask him to comment on it and then not have Dr. Karadzic also be able to comment on the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I didn't get the chance to ask the witness to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: True -- it was true that Ms. Gustafson didn't ask the witness to comment upon the document, so let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I'll start with the most recent things. Mr. Radan, can you tell us when this crossing over took place and when these 300 people had gathered together?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I said that it happened on the morning of 30th of September, early in the morning, and most probably they assembled immediately prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to everything that you know, how many people would it require to forcibly take 300 people out of their houses and expel them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be certain about that, but it will definitely need a large group of people if they wanted to expel them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether these civilians took some personal belongings with them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Believe me, I have no information about that, because I never saw them crossing over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard that there was a lot of commotion, that there was or big crowd, that 300 people were assembled in one spot --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the answer given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely agree with Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Strike that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 48, you were asked about instruction A or B. Did you follow this instruction A and B in executing your power? I'm talking about transcript page, not the page from your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson, before Mr. Radan answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The witness's testimony on instruction A and B was that he didn't know anything about it, so if Dr. Karadzic wants to ask whether it was followed, then he should lay some foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think he's entitled to answer that question. If foundation is required from the answer he can follow up on that, but that seemed to be a very legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he not say that he didn't know that document at the time of distribution? Mr. Radan, did you become aware of that document at any point of time later on? The content of it, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was a meeting on the 21st of December, 1991, in the Vraca local commune. There I was appointed to the local commune board on behalf of the SDS. At that meeting, the security situation was discussed. Among other things, I mentioned a case where my car were broken into and the seats torn. That was one of the remarks I made. The rest applied to the security situation and the presence of the police in charge of that area who were trying to act without bias. We asked those superior to him to have him removed from our area, but this paper that was mentioned was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my question was whether you became aware of the document later on, 1992 or 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Karadzic, you see the point of Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He could have answered no to that question, which would have also made the same point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not knowing the document how could he say that -- whether he was implementing the decisions or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He could say that their decisions were being made not following that document and other grounds. That's what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, let's not discuss it. He said he didn't know the content of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies -- Your Excellencies, if you only trusted me more, you would see its relevance. I wanted to ask him whether anyone from the authorities wanted to check whether they acted on this, but now it's moot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 50 of the transcript, you were asked about a meeting concerning the defence of Garici [phoen]. As far as you know about our laws and state administration, can you tell us whether a municipality has genuine competence in the domain of defence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was operational at the time, and it had competence to organise people in terms of self-protection in order to prevent anarchy and disorder and to protect the population from security incidents. That's their role as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under the law of All People's Defence, did the municipal president and the Assembly speaker have any competence in the area of defence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: They were competent to provide infrastructure, the conditions necessary to mount a defence. That was it. The rest was up to the army and probably the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they then have to attend meetings called by the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Well, in any case, they should have a common interest, and we responded to each of their invitation as they did when we invited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 55 and 56, it was suggested to you that at Vraca there was a special force the MUP. Vraca, that is to say Grbavica, was it within the area of responsibility of that brigade, and what was the nature of that brigade? Was it a mobile brigade or territorial one?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: They were in Vraca for a short while only. Before the conflict broke out, they happened to have been there, whereas later they moved to Lukavica and elsewhere. As for the police school premises, international forces, including UNPROFOR, were later billeted there. So the unit was mobile and sent where needed. They were not deployed in that area alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the soldiers who were defending Grbavica, were they accommodated in garrison or barracks conditions? In their free time did they spend their days in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Some, but most of them went home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't think this arises from the cross-examination nor does it seem to be particularly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you not ask the police power and military existence in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So if you believe that the question is relevant to that, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think so. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you were asked and shown that at the meeting, there was discussion of soldiers committing crimes, was it also stated that such acts were committed by units or individuals in their spare time when off duty?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: To my knowledge, they were committed by individuals when they were off duty, but it's an opinion of mine. It wasn't discussed in terms of Grbavica per se but generally, and it had to do with what the officers had to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Exhibit P5065 on page 8 that was shown to you -- well, I wanted to read out a portion starting with the words or remarks of late Mr. Prijic. In the English it is page 12. It reads as follows: "There are certain problems, thefts, and shooting by fighters. It would be very useful to obtain assistance from the army in order to prevent such problematic behaviour." Then another sentence: "Many fighters act wilfully. They are taking away property en masse and forcing people out of their apartments. It is not being sanctioned and affects the morale. The military police has been tackling the problem but they are still not enough in terms of numbers." Is that what you would agree with?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpret's note: There was no pause. Could the witness repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Radan, please put a pause before starting answering the question. The interpreters were not able to hear your answer. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I do not agree in full with what President Prijic stated. That was his own observation. I disagree with it, because that was not the case in Grbavica, and this was not the only case where we did not share the same view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radan, did you disagree with his opinion of the situation or with his assertion that the military police was still too weak?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I disagreed with his image of the situation. The military police was set up in Grbavica when Mr. Sipcic arrived. The military police was established partially in Grbavica, and they acted whenever necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You meant General Sipcic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: No, Mr. Simo Sipcic who was chief of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have in e-court page -- yes. Yes. Can we have 1D2799, if that is an exhibit already. No, it hasn't been admitted. Perhaps we shall tender it shortly. 1D2799.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So let me tell you about the document. This purports to be a statement by Mr. Simo Sipcic in the media. He stated that Novo Sarajevo rule of law is being established. In the municipality of Novo Sarajevo public law and order is gradually being established according to the statement of Captain Simo Sipcic, chief of the military police of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo. Civilians respect the military and civilian authorities. All difficulties that the citizens had are -- were being effectively dealt with regardless of their nationality. The number of citizens returning illegally obtained property to the authorities is ever-increasing, et cetera, does this tally with Mr. Sipcic's attempts to introduce law and order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: Yes, it does, in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what appears to be happening -- this document was notified to us as a document that the accused was planning to use in direct and if fits squarely within the testimony that the accused elicited from the witness. What appears to be happening here is that the accused is holding back eliciting some of this evidence and then waiting until after the cross-examination and attempting to somehow rehabilitate the witness with questions that are basically duplicative of the direct examination. That's not what redirect examination is for. It's supposed to be narrowly directed to specific issues that arise directly from the cross-examination and that's not what's going on here, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the redirect examination is limited by the scope of the cross, and when she goes into areas like this which she clearly did, then Dr. Karadzic is entitled. He can choose to forego a document in his direct examination and then later decide to use it if it's within the scope of cross. There's nothing wrong with that at all. This is a trial where both sides get a chance to do that. The Prosecution did that whenever they felt they had the need to do that for reasons of time or whatever. So I don't see that that's a valid objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By doing so, if the Defence is going to elicit a new element, the Prosecution should be allowed to cross-examine that part as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson. Let's continue. Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on page 8, you agreed that they were consulted but still inefficient, the military police, that is. Did they distinguish among the citizens of Novo Sarajevo based on their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge. Everyone had the right. Mr. Simo Sipcic was open to all remarks and objections. Anyone could approach him and lodge a complaint. There was no discrimination that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one question that remains unclear concerning the Jewish Cemetery. Did the confrontation line have to do with the Jewish Cemetery? Where were the forces of the two sides?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN
utterances.text: It was at the foot of Debelo Brdo. That's where the Jewish Cemetery is including Gornji Kovacici and Donji Kovacici and the lines went all the way to the Vrbanja Bridge. That was the separation line, and there was basically daily combat. From the Jewish Cemetery there were Muslim forces shooting, and on the other side there were the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll give the next Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number D2552, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Gustafson, for complimenting me on my skill to be able to manipulate evidence. Unfortunately, I'm still an amateur. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Radan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Radan. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we bring in the next witness, shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guzina. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Guzina, before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I said "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guzina. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Guzina.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: I probably did. Can you tell me which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we have 1D607 [as interpreted]. I had the written statement in mind. Also, please put a break between questions and answers so as not to wear out the interpreters and have an accurate record. 1D6807.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the statement and sign it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it contain accurately everything you said or would you change anything?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, it's all in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers be the same basically?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: They would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I like to tender this statement on the basis of Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About the documents -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would ask that five of the documents be added to our 65 ter list. The reason they were not on the list is that we weren't aware of them at the time that the initial interview was -- at the time that the exhibit list was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Five or six, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There are six exhibits but five are not on the list. One is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which was on the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: 1D01762, the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Any objections? Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit the 92 ter statement first. We'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6807 receives number D2553, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the -- as regards the six associated exhibits, the numbers will be given in due course by the Registrar. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to read out the summary of your statement, Mr. Guzina's statement in the English language. [In English] Svetozar Guzina was the battalion commander of the 5th Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of the VRS beginning on the 22nd of June, 1992, and later the battalion commander for the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade. He served as a deputy brigade commander when the Ilidza Brigade commander was absent or on leave. Svetozar Guzina noted that in the spring of 1991, the Muslims in Sokolovic Kolonija had begun arming themselves. A few Serbs received threats that they would be expelled from Sokolovic Kolonija and they became very concerned. In an attempt to resolve the situation a meeting was set up with prominent representatives of the three peoples, Svetozar Guzina became a representative of the Serb people. At the meeting, the Muslim representatives originally denied that they were arming, an agreement was reached that a joint night-time patrol should be set up to reassure the population. In late February 1992, barricades were erected which stopped people leaving Sokolovic Kolonija. Muslims became more vocal and began demonstrating against the Serbs. In March 1992, a large crowd of armed Muslims gathered by the primary school in Sokolovic Kolonija. When Svetozar Guzina arrived, he and those with him were forced out of the car and were searched by armed men. They were held at gunpoint and Svetozar Guzina was certain he was going to die. Enver Hodzic, one of the representatives of the Muslims, and Husein Mahmutovic, who was president of the municipality, calmed the situation down and they were released. After this incident the situation deteriorated and more barricades were erected. The Serb population was surrounded. The Serbian authorities in Ilidza concluded that Serbs should move out of Sokolovic Kolonija while a large number of Serbs had already left their homes. A further meeting was held at which the Muslims suggested Serbs not to leave their own homes as the Muslims would guarantee their safety and peace and would protect the Serb population. However, Svetozar Guzina no longer had faith in the guarantees provided by the Muslims. At the meeting, armed men burst in reporting a further incident in Foca during which people had been killed and injured, tensions were very high. It was decided that Enver Hodzic, a Muslim representative, and Svetozar Guzina should make an announcement on the radio to the people of Sokolovic Kolonija in an attempt to stop the fighting. Svetozar Guzina heard from his brother that the world media was reporting that there would be a war in BH. He found that some sort of League for Yugoslavia existed and it attracted people from all ethnic backgrounds. The league handed out weapons to Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. The first attack on Ilidza took place on 22nd of April, 1992, when Muslims entered the hospital and took doctors and patients prisoners. They then began shooting from the building. Svetozar Guzina and those with him had no previous experience of battle and many were shooting out of fear. The battle lasted until 5.00 p.m. when the JNA arrived from Lukavica and this is when the shooting stopped. Many were relieved by the arrival of the army. The fighting continued for a number of months with daily battles raging and during this period they were trained by the JNA. There were no plans to advance at this point, simply to defend their own property and their lives. During the fighting across B and H, the police basically fell apart and the army in Sarajevo was attacked and practically destroyed. Many people were captured, killed, or wounded. The army did not come to assist in Ilidza. Many people did not have regular meals and they were very scared. In June 1992, the JNA were involved in a deliberation of residential area in Dobrinja near the airport, without which the unit would be basically surrounded with only one road towards Pale accessible to them. The Muslims responded to these movements during a cease-fire with a fierce counter attack. Svetozar Guzina requested artillery from the Igman Brigade which was granted once extensive explanations were -- immediately after extensive explanations were given about the reasons for this request. Svetozar Guzina never issued an order to fire at civilians, nor was he aware that any of his subordinates or superiors issued such an order. Each commander of a unit was to evacuate civilians from the zone of combat operation or limit their presence in these zones. However, civilians continued to remain near the front line despite the warnings. Svetozar Guzina was aware that Muslim forces had positions in civilian zones and civilian buildings throughout the fighting, including the television building, Fatima Gunic school, Dobrinja C5, and Papagajka building.
